name: Aluminum chloride prescription (Drysol)

lead: Prescription aluminium chloride is for people whose sweat shows through clothes: it aims for dry underarms, hands or feet and far fewer sweat stains.

It is a stronger form of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, blocking sweat ducts so less sweat reaches the skin. Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy for hyperhidrosis, and improvement is reported to take about three to five days.

paras: Prescribed by a clinician for hyperhidrosis and applied to dry skin on the affected area, typically as the step after over-the-counter antiperspirants stop being enough.
Skin irritation is the most common side effect. The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor first. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Prescription aluminium chloride is used for heavy sweating to stay dry and avoid visible sweat marks and odor. It blocks sweat ducts, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line hyperhidrosis therapy.

lead: Drysol is a brand of prescription topical aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating.[1] Aluminium chloride is a stronger version of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy.[1]

Wikipedia reports that improvement takes about three to five days and that the most common side effect is skin irritation.[1] In appearance culture it matters mainly to people concerned with visible underarm, hand or foot sweat.

paras: Hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8% of the US population, most often appearing between ages 25 and 64, with a family history in 30 to 50 percent of cases.[1] Higher-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants have shown some success for hand and foot sweating.[1]
Skin irritation is the most common side effect.[1] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[2]
Wikipedia cites Everdry as the first commercial antiperspirant in 1903.[2] Specific details about Drysol's development were not found in the sources loaded.

No studies found specific to Drysol in the sources loaded; the Hyperhidrosis article cites an evidence-based review of nonsurgical management and guidelines from the International Hyperhidrosis Society without giving trial results.[1]

timeline.event: Everdry, the first commercial antiperspirant, marketed.[2]
